$comment: Answering CTCP. Shared by tests/shared/ctcp.test.ts and the Android SharedCorpusTest, so a person who asks a desktop, a phone and an always-on instance the same question gets the same answer. Switchboard used to ignore CTCP asked of a channel, which is how people ask — a survey got a reply from every client in the room except this one.
$replies: verb and args in, the NOTICE body out, or null for something we do not answer.

replies.name: source, the one they ask next
clientinfo names the rest
replies.reply: CLIENTINFO CLIENTINFO PING SOURCE TIME VERSION

replies.name: time, to the second and spelled the same on both
ping comes back exactly as it went
an empty ping is still a ping
finger, which nobody should still be asking
an unknown verb with a payload is not answered either

$kinds: What a line wrapped in \u0001 is. Three things arrive looking alike and the phone told only two of them apart: a CTCP reply was filed as an ordinary notice, which opened a direct message with whoever answered — and where the reply was our own, echoed back, with the person who had asked us. A reply goes in the console and never opens a conversation.

kinds.name: an ordinary line is not CTCP
a question asked of this client
ACTION is matched whatever its case
ACTION with nothing after it is not one
an answer comes back as a NOTICE
a NOTICE is an answer whatever verb it carries
an ordinary notice is not CTCP
one wrapped end is not a wrapping

$answerLines: How an answer reads in the console. It is two clients talking rather than two people, which is why it goes there and not into a conversation.

answerLines.name: the verb is named as the convention writes it
nothing inside the wrapping
